items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the election law, in relation to the confidentiality of
registration records for victims of domestic violence
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S1555

SPONSOR: MYRIE
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the election law, in relation to the confidentiality of
registration records for victims of domestic violence

 
PURPOSE:

To ensure that the home addresses of domestic violence survivors is not
made public through voter records.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 of the bill amends Subdivision 2 of section 5-508 of the
election law to allow for a victim of domestic violence to opt in to
voter confidentiality by delivering to the Board of Elections a signed
written statement swearing or affirming:

* That they are the victim of domestic violence
* That because of the threat of physical or emotional harm to themself
or to family or household members, they wish for their registration
record to be kept confidential.

The Board of Election must keep this information confidential Section 2
establishes the effective date of the bill.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Under current New York law, all voter records are public domain. This
makes a voter's place of residence publicly accessible to anyone who
knows how to search for it. If an abuse or domestic violence survivor
were to register to vote, their home address would become public and
readily available to an abuser, placing them in further danger. The
state's current voter confidentiality program requires the survivor go
to court to apply for confidentiality. This onerous, time consuming, and
difficult process leaves the burden on survivors and can oftentimes bar
them from safely registering to vote and exercising their constitutional
rights.

According to the CDC, 1 in 4 women and 1 in 7 men will experience severe
physical violence by an intimate partner in their lifetime.  The public
availability of voter information disenfranchises vulnerable New Yorkers
who are unable to register to vote without putting themselves in danger.

Further, survivors who are unaware that their residence is publicly
available are at risk.

This legislation would allow survivors to opt to have their voter
records private for their safety by signing an affidavit that they are a
survivor of domestic violence. This option would continue to allow for
localities to verify the voter's information while protecting them from
exposing their place of residence to their abuser. This change would
mimic the language and threshold for entry used in section 11-306 of the
election law which provides that a victim of domestic violence can
submit a written statement swearing or affirming they are a victim of
domestic violence and need a special ballot. This bill would streamline

the election law and provide the same standard for both sections of the
law.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

Originally Assembly Bill 11052.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

Not yet determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.
